context.problemStatement:
Implement the `Lambda` case of `eval`. An anonymous function `fn(x) { ... }`
evaluates to a function value. Nothing in its body is evaluated until it is
called, so this case never returns an error. Build a `VFunc(UserFn(...))` whose
name is `"lambda"` (used in error messages) and whose parent is the environment
in which this function was *defined*, not the one in which it will be called. This
is what lets a function use the names around it, even after the call that created it
has returned.

```
// In eval:
    Lambda(params, body) ->
      // YOUR CODE HERE (replace the code below)
      Error(errors.NotImplemented(
        "Lambda("
        <> string.inspect(params)
        <> ", "
        <> string.inspect(body)
        <> ")",
      ))
```

Run the tests:

```
gleam test -- q8
```

targets.claim: Student can explain why their Lambda case never returns an error even when the body of the anonymous function uses an unbound name, and when such an error would appear instead.

probes.question: If `body` in your `Lambda(params, body)` case references an unbound variable, why does evaluating `Lambda(params, body)` still return `Ok` without an error, and when would that error actually get raised?
probes.reason: Directly checks whether the student understands that lambda creation does not evaluate the body and that unbound variable errors are deferred until application.

probes.question: Why doesn't your `Lambda(params, body)` arm call `eval` on `body`, and what would have to happen in the program for `body` to finally be evaluated?
probes.reason: Tests the same deferred evaluation concept by asking about the lack of an `eval` call on `body` and when that evaluation eventually happens.

content: If `body` in your `Lambda(params, body)` case references an unbound variable, why does evaluating `Lambda(params, body)` still return `Ok` without an error, and when would that error actually get raised?
evaluating a lambda just saves the function; it doesnt run the body code yet. the unbound variable error is only raised later when you actually call the function and the body gets ealuated

reason: The student correctly explained that evaluating a lambda only constructs/saves the function without evaluating its body, and that the unbound variable error is only raised later when the function is called and the body evaluated.
